To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

mAbs that act by mimicking the natural ligand are agonist antibodies, and that mAbs that bind to a site that is topographically distinct from that of the natural ligand, but which modulates receptor function, are antagonists.
(i) the Fc domain of mAbs is essential for their agonistic activity, and (ii) the agonistic activity of mAbs is mediated by the Fab domain, which mimics the natural ligand.

(i) mAbs can be used to stimulate the immune response, (ii) the stimulation of immune effector mechanisms can be enhanced by the simultaneous stimulation of the antigen receptor, (iii) the stimulation of antigen receptors can be enhanced by simultaneous crosslinking with mAbs, and (iv) the stimulation of receptors is not restricted to B cells and T cells, but is also observed in other cell types, including hematopoietic and non-hematopoietic cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of mAbs as agonists/antagonists, with the ultimate goal of developing therapeutic agents for human disease.
the design of antibodies that can be applied in the clinic as agonists or antagonists of receptors that are relevant for the pathogenesis of human diseases.
the potential therapeutic use of antibodies that can act as agonists or antagonists for receptors that regulate immune and inflammatory responses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
mAbs can be agonists or antagonists, depending on the receptor they bind and the nature of their binding site.

antibodies can be used to mimic natural ligands and to activate signaling pathways, and that the therapeutic potential of such mAbs can be further exploited by the development of bispecific molecules that can bind two antigens and activate signaling pathways.
mAb agonists and antagonizers are not a new concept, but rather an expansion of the therapeutic potential of mAb-based therapies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
mAbs can be designed to act as agonists or antagonists of a variety of receptors.
the use of agonistic mAbs as therapeutics is an exciting new field of research, and the potential clinical applications of such molecules are enormous.
the use of mAbs as surrogate agonists is an attractive strategy in the treatment of human diseases.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of mAbs as receptor agonists/antagonists is a promising approach in the field of applied medicine.

the use of agonistic antibodies is a powerful approach to treat diseases, and that this approach is likely to expand as the number of receptors with known ligands increases, and the number of receptors that have not yet been characterized increases.

mAbs can be engineered to mimic ligand binding and hence activate receptor-mediated signaling pathways, or they can be designed to antagonize agonistic signaling by competing with the endogenous agonist.
